html:
Somapura Mahavihara, at Paharpur in northwestern Bangladesh, is a great Buddhist monastery built in the late 8th century by Dharmapala, king of the Pala Empire.

Its square court, about 280 metres a side, was ringed by 177 monks' cells around a tall cross-shaped temple, decorated with terracotta plaques of daily life, animals and gods. It was among the largest monasteries in South Asia and stood with Nalanda and Vikramashila as a centre of learning in the last great age of Indian Buddhism. Atisha, who later took Buddhism to Tibet, is said to have stayed there.

The monastery was burned in the 11th century and slowly abandoned as Buddhism faded in Bengal. Its plan is thought to have influenced temples in Burma and Java. Since 1985 it has been a World Heritage Site, the best known ruin in Bangladesh.
sum: Somapura Mahavihara, at Paharpur in northwestern Bangladesh, is a great Buddhist monastery built in the late 8th century by Dharmapala, king of the Pala Empire.
